# Volume 2 — V A Full-fledged Schoolma’am

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

As Nell arrived at the school on that morning . . . having traveled the Aspen Path for the very first time in her life oblivious and unseeing to its charm . . . everything was calm and motionless. The former instructor had taught the pupils to be seated upon her coming, and as Nell stepped into the classroom she was met by neat lines of “shining morning faces” and gleaming, curious eyes. Hanging up her hat, she turned toward her students, trusting that she did not appear as terrified and silly as she felt inside and that they would fail to notice how her body shook.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0000 }

She had remained awake until almost midnight on the previous evening drafting an address that she intended to deliver to her students when school commenced. Having meticulously edited and refined the piece, she subsequently committed it to memory. It was an excellent address containing several truly wonderful concepts, particularly regarding shared assistance and the diligent pursuit of learning. Its sole defect was her present inability to recall any part of it.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0001 }

Following what felt like a year to her—though it was actually roughly ten seconds—she whispered weakly, “Take your Testaments, please,” and dropped out of breath into her seat behind the noise of desktop lids opening and slamming that came next. As the verses were being read by the children, Nell rallied her trembling thoughts into place and surveyed the assembled small travelers bound for the Grownup Land.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0002 }

Naturally, the majority of them were already very familiar to her. Although her personal classmates had graduated during the previous year, she had attended school alongside all the others, with the exception of the primer class and ten individuals who were new to Brierley. Nell harbored a covert curiosity regarding these ten that surpassed her interest in those whose potential was already reasonably clear to her. Granted, they could turn out to be every bit as ordinary as the others; nevertheless, it was also possible that a genius was in their midst. The thought was electrifying.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0003 }

Anthony Tulk was seated alone at a desk in the corner. His small face was dark and gloomy, and he glared at Nell, his black eyes filled with enmity. Right then, Nell resolved to gain the boy’s love and completely defeat the Tulks.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0004 }

Sitting with Arty Mott in the opposite corner was one more unusual boy . . . a merry-faced little fellow, who had a snub nose, a face covered in freckles, and large, pale blue eyes that were bordered by whitish eyelashes . . . likely the Trask boy; and if there was any truth in a likeness, his sister was seated with Mary Bell across the aisle. Nell pondered the nature of the child's mother, who would allow her to go to school wearing such clothes. A washed-out pink dress made of silk was what she had on, adorned with an abundance of cotton lace, dirty white slippers of kid leather, and stockings of silk. Her sandy-colored hair had been twisted into countlessly tight and unnatural curls, topped by an extravagant pink ribbon bow that exceeded the size of her head. Based on her look, she felt extremely pleased with her appearance.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0005 }

A faint, small child, whose shoulders were draped in sleek waves of soft, delicate, fawn-hued hair, Nell reasoned, had to be Annetta Bell, a girl whose mother and father used to reside within the Stonebridge school area, yet, because they dragged their home fifty yards to the north of its previous location, currently belonged to Brierley. A trio of sickly-looking little girls jammed together in a single desk were unquestionably Cottons; while there could be no uncertainty that the little belle boasting extended brown ringlets and hazel-colored eyes, who threw flirtatious glances toward Jack Gills from behind her Testament, was Prillie Rogerson, a child whose father had lately taken a second spouse and fetched Prillie back to the area from the residence of her grandmother located in Welby. A lanky, ungainly girl positioned in a rear desk, who appeared to possess an excess of feet and hands, Nell was completely unable to identify, though she subsequently learned that she was called Barbara Shaw and had arrived to reside alongside an aunt residing in Brierley. Nell was likewise destined to learn that whenever Barbara succeeded in navigating the aisle without tripping over her own boots or those belonging to someone else, the Brierley pupils recorded that exceptional occurrence upon the wall of the porch to mark the event.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0006 }

However, as Nell’s gaze connected with the eyes of the boy sitting at the front desk opposite hers, a strange small tremor passed through her, as though her genius had been discovered. It was clear to her that this had to be Cedric Stanhope and that, on this occasion, Mrs. Agatha Sowerby had accurately predicted his unlikeness to the Brierley children. Beyond that, it hit Nell that he was different from other children in any place, and that a soul delicately related to hers was staring back at her from the extremely dark blue eyes observing her with such fixed attention.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0007 }

Although aware that Cedric was ten years old, she thought he appeared to be at most eight. In her eyes, his tiny face was the most beautiful she had ever observed on a child . . . displaying features of delicate and exquisite refinement surrounded by a halo of chestnut curls. Full without any pout, his mouth was delicious, with crimson lips that barely touched each other and curved into finely crafted tiny corners that almost formed dimples. A sober, grave, and meditative expression was upon him, as though his spirit possessed much greater age than his body; however, the moment Nell gave him a soft smile, that look disappeared into an abrupt responsive smile that appeared to illuminate his entire being, like an internal lamp suddenly lighting into a flame that irradiated him from head to foot. Best of all, this reaction was involuntary, arising from no outer motive or effort, but merely the outward flash of a concealed personality that was fine, sweet, and rare. Through this swift exchange of smiles, Nell and Cedric became fast friends forever prior to any words passing between them.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0008 }

The day passed as though it were a dream, and Nell was unable to distinctly remember it later on. It felt nearly as if someone other than herself was doing the teaching. Mechanically, she set copies, worked sums, and heard classes. Quite well-behaved, the children presented only two instances requiring discipline. Morley Pullen received a catching while steering a team of trained crickets down the aisle. Nell made Morley stand upon the platform for an hour and—an act Morley felt far more deeply—took away his crickets. Having placed them inside a box, she liberated them at Primrose Dell as she walked home from school; nevertheless, Morley thought, both at that time and perpetually after, that she carried them to her home to keep for her personal entertainment.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0009 }

Anthony Tulk was the second offender, emptying the final drops of water contained in his slate bottle onto the back of Aurelia Clay’s neck. Keeping Anthony inside during recess, Nell discussed with him how gentlemen ought to behave, warning him that ladies’ necks were never to have water poured down them by such men. She explained that it was her wish for every one of her boys to become a gentleman. Quite kind and touching though her brief lecture was, Anthony was regrettably left entirely unaffected. Maintaining a silent posture alongside his unchanged sullen look, he listened to her, letting out a contemptuous whistle upon his departure. Nell let out a sigh, but she subsequently raised her own spirits by recalling that earning the regard of a Tulk was not accomplished in a single day, much like the construction of Rome. Indeed, whether certain Tulks possessed any affections capable of being won remained questionable; nevertheless, Nell held higher expectations for Anthony, whose appearance suggested he could be a fairly pleasant boy if his sullen exterior were ever penetrated.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0010 }

Once school had been let out and the pupils were gone, Nell sank exhaustedly into her seat. A headache plagued her, and a profound sense of disheartening weight came over her. No genuine cause existed for such despair, given that no truly terrible incident had transpired; nonetheless, Nell suffered from deep fatigue and was disposed to think that developing a fondness for pedagogy was beyond her. Furthermore, spending each day engaged in an unappealing occupation for . . . say, four decades, struck her as an appalling prospect. Nell hesitated between weeping immediately on the spot, or postponing her tears until she reached the security of her own white bedroom at home. Prior to reaching a choice, the sound of tapping heels and the rustle of silk sounded across the porch floor, bringing Nell face to face with a woman whose attire brought to mind a comment Mr. Pettifer had lately made regarding a excessively adorned woman he observed within a Port Marlow shop. “She looked like a head-on collision between a fashion plate and a nightmare.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0011 }

The late arrival had put on a magnificent pale blue summer silk outfit, which was puffed, frilled, and shirred in every conceivable spot where puffing, frilling, or shirring could be added. Sitting atop her head was an enormous white chiffon hat, adorned with three extended yet somewhat scrawny ostrich feathers. A veil made of pink chiffon, generously dotted with gigantic black spots, draped down like a flounce from the brim of the hat to her shoulders, drifting behind her in a pair of light streamers. She was decked out in as much jewelry as a single petite woman could fit upon herself, and a powerful scent of perfume accompanied her.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0012 }

“I am Mrs. Trask . . . Mrs. H. B. Trask,” declared this sight, “and the reason I have visited you is regarding an issue Clarice Almira mentioned to me upon returning home for dinner today. It caused me extreme annoyance.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0013 }

“I’m sorry,” Nell stammered, attempting without success to recall a single event from that morning involving the Trask children.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0014 }

“Clarice Almira mentioned to me that you said our name was Trask. However, Miss Harcourt, Trask is the proper way to pronounce our name . . . with the stress placed on the final syllable. I trust you will keep this in mind going forward.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0015 }

“I will attempt to,” Nell panted, suppressing a hysterical urge to giggle. “It is very disagreeable to have a person's name misspelled, as I have learned firsthand, and I imagine having it mispronounced is likely still more dreadful.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0016 }

“Of course it is. Furthermore, Clarice Almira let me know that you address my son as Jacob.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0017 }

“Jacob was the name he gave me,” Nell objected.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0018 }

“I might have expected that,” Mrs. H. B. Trask said, using a voice suggesting that one could not anticipate thankfulness from youth in these fallen times. “That boy possesses very common preferences, Miss Harcourt. At his birth, my wish was to name him St. Clair . . . it has such an aristocratic ring, doesn't it? His father, however, demanded that he be named Jacob after his uncle. I gave in, since Uncle Jacob happened to be a wealthy old bachelor. And what do you imagine, Miss Harcourt? Once our blameless child reached five years of age, Uncle Jacob went ahead and took a wife, and he currently possesses three sons himself. Have you ever known such a lack of appreciation? As soon as the wedding invitation . . . because he possessed the audacity to mail us an invitation, Miss Harcourt . . . arrived at our home, I said, ‘No more Jacobs for me, thank you.’ Ever since that day, I referred to my son as St. Clair, and I am resolved that St. Clair is what he must be named. His father stubborn-headedly keeps calling him Jacob, while the youth himself displays a completely baffling liking for that coarse name. Nevertheless, he is St. Clair, and St. Clair he will continue to be. You will be good enough to bear this in mind, Miss Harcourt, won't you? Thank you. I informed Clarice Almira of my certainty that this was merely a misinterpretation which a single word would fix. Trask. . . stress the final syllable . . . and St. Clair . . . under no circumstances Jacob. You will keep this in mind? Thank you.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0019 }

Once Mrs. H. B. Trask had glided off, Nell secured the door of the school and headed home. Near the base of the hill, she encountered Cedric Stanhope beside the Aspen Path. He presented her with a bunch of the delicate small wild orchids that young ones in Brierley named “rice lillies.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0020 }

“I ask you to take these, teacher, which I discovered in the field belonging to Mr. Duckett,” he uttered bashfully, “and I returned so I could offer them to you since I believed you were a lady who would appreciate them, and also because . . .” he raised his large, gorgeous eyes . . . “teacher, I am fond of you.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0021 }

“You darling,” said Nell, as she took the scented blooms. Just as though a magical spell had been cast by Cedric’s words, tiredness and gloom left her soul, while a surge of hope, like a fountain dancing, rose within her heart. She walked along the Aspen Path with light steps, accompanied by the sweet perfume of her orchids as if receiving a blessing.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0022 }

“So, what progress did you make?” Thirza inquired.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0023 }

“Inquire about that in a month’s time and I might be capable of informing you. At present I am unable to . . . I do not know personally . . . I am excessively close to it. It feels as though my thoughts were completely churned about until they became dense and murky. The single matter I am truly certain of achieving today is my teaching Cliffie Duckett that A is A. Prior to this, he was unaware of it. Is it not an achievement to have set a soul upon a route that might terminate in Shakespeare and Paradise Lost?”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0024 }

Afterwards, Mrs. Sowerby arrived bringing additional cheer. At her gate, that kind woman had stopped the pupils from school and asked them what they thought of their new instructor.
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0025 }

“And each single one of them stated they liked you splendid, Nell, with the exception of Anthony Tulk. I have to confess he failed to. He stated you ‘weren’t any good, just like all girl teachers.’ There is the Tulk leaven for you. But do not mind.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0026 }

“I will not mind,” Nell said softly, “and Anthony Tulk will come to like me eventually. He will certainly be won over by patience and kindness.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0027 }

“Indeed, predicting what a Tulk might do is impossible,” Mrs. Agatha remarked guardedly. “More often than not, they act in opposition to expectations, much like dreams. Regarding that Trask woman, I certainly won't be referring to her as Donnelling, you may be certain of that. Trask is her name and always was. In my opinion, the woman is simply insane. She owns a pug dog named Queenie who sits at the dinner table with the rest of the family, consuming its food from a china plate. Were I in her shoes, I would fear divine punishment. Thomas considers Trask himself to be a practical, industrious man, though he believes he lacked good sense when selecting a spouse.”
{: #nw-v02-c05-p0028 }
